analysis.one_liner: Requires any food containing or produced with genetically engineered material to carry a clear 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' label.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committees without ever receiving a vote, despite 17 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal food, meat, and poultry laws so that any food containing or made with genetically engineered material — including meat and poultry from animals fed engineered feed — could not legally be sold without a prominent 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' label on the package. It would also have required periodic government testing along the supply chain to verify label accuracy, set civil fines up to $100,000 per violation, and let ordinary citizens sue to enforce the rule. Restaurant meals and food prepared fresh in retail stores were exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who want to know what is in their food — including people with allergen concerns, religious or ethical dietary restrictions, and shoppers who prefer to avoid engineered ingredients. Farmers and food companies producing non-engineered and certified organic food would also benefit, because the bill gave them a federal standard for claiming their products are engineered-free and exempted certified organic foods from the testing requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Grocery shoppers and organic food producers

how_it_helps.text: Any food containing or produced with genetically engineered material would be misbranded — illegal to sell — unless labeled with the notices 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' and 'THIS PRODUCT CONTAINS A GENETICALLY ENGINEERED MATERIAL, OR WAS PRODUCED WITH A GENETICALLY ENGINEERED MATERIAL' in a conspicuous size comparable to nutrition labels.

The bill applied the same rule to meat and poultry, treating animals fed genetically engineered feed as 'produced with' engineered material, so the label would reach most commodity meat, corn, and soy products, not just items with engineered ingredients.

Regulations would require periodic testing of foods as they moved through the chain of distribution to verify label accuracy, with certified organic foods exempt from testing and a 1% tolerance for accidental contamination.

The bill authorized citizen suits — letting any person go to court against violators or against the Secretary for failing to enforce the rules — and set civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, while shielding producers whose crops were unintentionally contaminated and buyers who relied in good faith on a supplier's guarantee.

The bill's findings stated that labels voluntarily placed on foods were insufficient, that consumers had a right to know for health, environmental, religious, and ethical reasons, and that major trading partners including the EU, Japan, and China already had or were implementing mandatory labeling — which the bill said would help American farmers export to those markets.

analysis.who_pays: Food and agricultural companies that use genetically engineered ingredients or feed: seed and biotech developers, commodity grain and livestock producers, and packaged-food manufacturers, who would bear labeling costs, supply-chain testing, and the risk of $100,000-per-violation fines and citizen lawsuits. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Biotech, grain, meat, and packaged-food companies

drawbacks.text: The trigger is broad: because most corn, soy, and sugar beet crops and most animal feed in the U.S. are genetically engineered, the bill would effectively require labeling on a very large share of packaged foods and on meat from animals fed engineered feed, a compliance burden spanning the entire supply chain.

The bill imposed civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation on the food label itself, plus citizen suits with attorney-fee awards, which small food businesses could find costly even where the underlying labeling change is cheap.

A good-faith objection supporters would have to answer: the label applies to foods from animals merely fed engineered grain, and to products where the engineered trait itself is not detectable in the final ingredient, so the label conveys production method rather than a difference in the food on the shelf — the kind of breadth that labeling opponents argued could lead shoppers to read a safety warning into a production-method disclosure. The bill responded by barring regulators from forcing 'non-GE' labels to carry disclaimers about safety.
Restaurant meals and food prepared fresh in retail stores were exempt, so the same engineered ingredient would be labeled in a packaged product but not in a restaurant dish.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is information at essentially the cost of printing a label, and the bill included genuine accommodations — organic exemption, a 1% contamination tolerance, guaranty protections for buyers, and an intent-based shield for farmers whose fields are accidentally cross-contaminated. The real burden falls on supply chains that would have to segregate and test to make labels accurate, and the animal-feed trigger makes that burden very large. Reasonable people can weigh disclosure against that compliance cost; what is not in dispute is that shoppers would have gotten information about engineered ingredients that they do not get today.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2006, referred to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees, sent to subcommittees, and never moved again — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the Genetically Engineered Food Right to Know Act on May 2, 2006, with 11 original cosponsors including Republicans Christopher Shays and以太 no — including Mr. Shays of Connecticut.
The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction.

Within weeks it was sent to three subcommittees: the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Agriculture subcommittees on Conservation, Credit, Rural Development, and Research and on Livestock and Horticulture.

After the subcommittee referrals in May 2006, no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 109th Congress, which ended January 3, 2007 — the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
The bill ended with 17 cosponsors: 15 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and biotech companies that sell engineered seeds and engineered-ingredient foods, which avoided mandatory labeling, supply-chain testing, and fines because the bill never advanced; shoppers never got the disclosure it would have required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food and biotech companies avoiding labels

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 17 cosponsors (15 Democrats, 1 Independent, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a small bipartisan base of support.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee and House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee and its subcommittees for eight months until the Congress ended.

against.name: Biotech seed and packaged-food industries
against.role: Industries affected by mandatory GE labeling
against.what_they_did: Long opposed federal mandatory labeling of genetically engineered foods, arguing such labels would stigmatize safe products and raise costs.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so positions were never tested on the floor; support was mostly Democratic but included a Republican (Christopher Shays) and an Independent (Bernie Sanders) among the cosponsors.

industries.note: Mandatory labeling plus supply-chain testing would have tagged nearly every commodity corn, soy, and cotton product derived from their seeds, and would have created a government-verified record distinguishing non-engineered crops — undercutting the status quo in which engineered foods are sold unlabeled. The bill dying meant no such disclosure requirement ever took effect.

They would have had to label or reformulate products and verify ingredients through the chain of distribution, facing fines up to $100,000 per violation and citizen suits. Their interest in avoiding these costs ran against shoppers' interest in knowing the ingredients.

industries.industry: Commodity livestock, meat, and poultry producers
industries.note: Because animals fed engineered grain counted as 'produced with' engineered material, most commodity meat and poultry would have needed the GE label, a cost the industry had no way to avoid without changing feed. Producers of certified non-GE meat would have gained a federal marketing standard instead.

Certified organic foods were exempt from testing, and any producer meeting the bill's rules could truthfully claim its food was not engineered-free-labeled-regulated — creating a federal standard that made avoiding engineered ingredients easier to verify and market to consumers.
